text: If the person is fully alert and able to swallow, I would give cyproheptadine early, since it blocks serotonin receptors. So far, the evidence for this med has only been case reports, and a recent review found them insufficient to show that it works. I wouldn't wait to see whether it does before doing the other steps. And most people won't have it at home anyway, since it needs a prescription in the US, though a telehealth doctor might write one quickly, and only some countries sell it without one.

marked.s: Most people won't have it at home anyway, since in the US it needs a prescription (a telehealth doctor might write one quickly), and only some countries sell it without one.
If they still show the signs of low electrolytes from MDMA:

Magnesium Alarm above, they may need a hypertonic electrolyte drink with more magnesium and potassium than a normal one, which can be as simple as a normal one with a bit of extra salt, potassium and magnesium thrown in, or a salty potato soup with some Epsom salt.
While you wait, you might think of this guide's other remedies, like niacin for ending a trip or DMSO for brain injuries, seizures and chest pain, but I wouldn't use either one here.
I'd also leave out this guide's Syrian rue oil for now: made at home it has almost none of the harmala alkaloids and might even help, but I couldn't find any research on it with MDMA.
Magnesium chloride is the one I would consider, since many people with serotonin syndrome run low on magnesium (a nursing review).
